lesson.title: Quest + Socratic Circle: Build It, Then Question It
lesson.topic: A multi-day hands-on project (a quest) ends with a Socratic discussion where learners answer questions instead of hearing answers.
lesson.steelman: Does a learner understand more by being told the answer or by being asked better questions?
lesson.steelman_for: Building something and then defending choices in a discussion makes learners think for themselves and remember far longer.
lesson.steelman_against: Discussion can stall without enough background knowledge, and confident talkers can dominate unless a guide keeps it fair.
lesson.example: Imagine Sam, 12, whose quest is to build a cardboard bridge that holds ten books. In the Socratic circle, the guide only asks questions like 'why did yours bend there?' and Sam explains triangles to the group.
lesson.activity: Pick a 2-3 day quest (bridge, garden box, simple circuit). When done, hold a 15-minute circle: a grown-up asks only questions (What worked? Why? What would you change? What would someone who disagrees say?).
check_questions: What makes a quest different from a worksheet?
In a Socratic circle, what does the guide do?
What is one question you would ask about someone else's project?
